newsitem.title: UK: Gold investors look to the skies with doubt.
newsitem.headline: Gold investors look to the skies with doubt.

text.p: When the Canadian exploration firm Bre-X Minerals Ltd announced the discovery of its Busang gold deposit in Indonesia, the find was soon dubbed the gold strike of the century.
After a run of exploration successes in recent years, investors clamoured for a stake, led by U.S. mining giant Freeport McMoRan Copper & Gold, which took a 15 percent share.

But more recent results from Freeport's own drilling, showing "insignificant" amounts of gold, sent Bre-X stock reeling and jolted investors generally into a more cautious approach to new finds in the future.
"In the short term people are going to find it difficult to value what we term the 'blue sky potential,'" said Jonathan de Thierry, mining analyst at HSBC James Capel in London.
Exploration successes such as Diamond Fields and Alumbrera had seen greed get the better of fear, analysts said, and to many market players the sky seemed the only limit to returns.

"There had become a feeling that this sort of thing happens often and that exploration stocks were an easy way to make money," said Roger Chaplin, head of research at T. Hoare and Co. stockbrokers in London.

Now investors will want evidence that exploration companies can fulfil their potential, analysts said. Comparisons with other samples from around the world will be needed before anyone jumps on a bandwagon.

If they are to be taken seriously in the future, other exploration companies may now be expected to produce detailed geological models of a sample to predict the amount and quality of wealth in the ground and prove a deposit's potential.
"Effectively, people are going to want to see hard evidence that the gold exists before they invest," de Thierry said.
It is essential that core samples be split in two, with half used for testing and half retained as a concrete example to return to, he added.
Though this is standard practice in gold exploration, the original Bre-X drilling sample disappeared.
But before it went missing, Bre-X used the sample to arrive at its estimate of 71 million ounces for the size of the Indonesia deposit, a huge amount in its own right.

And when the head of the exploration team said the Busang find could contain as much as 200 million ounces, expectations raced even higher, only to come crashing down to earth when Freeport carried out its own testing.
Analysts said investors would put a premium on caution in their examination of exploratory reports from now on.

"People have relied on the information given to them by the company as being reliable and now they are going to have to look at that much more carefully," said Martin Rosser, a director of David Williamson and Associates, a London-based consulting firm specialising in mining and minerals industries.
Several groups of Bre-X shareholders, outraged at the apparent inaccuracy of the assaying, are currently suing the company.
Rosser said investors would demand far higher standards in the sampling of future exploratory sites, and would be emphatic that external consultants play a greater role as projects develop.
Though there have been gold explorations that came to nothing in the past, analysts said the size of the Bre-X claims and the amount of people who believed in them have stunned the industry.
"What is different about Bre-X is the scale of it. With most companies who've seen problems like that before, it's not been a multi-billion dollar company," said Chaplin.
Bre-X shares rocketed on the Toronto Stock Exchange after the discovery of the Busang site, soon making it one of the largest gold companies in the world.
But when it was reported that Freeport's results might not match Bre-X's findings, Bre-X shares shed more than C$3 billion ($2.2 billion). They have since ceased trading.
The impact of the collapse in Bre-X shares has been industry-wide, with investor jitters spreading to many early-stage exploration companies, particularly in Canada.
Many such stocks have fallen by between 20 percent and 40 percent on the news, analysts said, and more losses were expected.
"People are using a scatter-gun approach and saying 'well, anything that's grass roots exploration, we're going to be much more cautious on,'" said Chaplin.
Analysts agreed that the Bre-X story had made investors far more cautious in the short-term. But before long they could soon be tempted again by the prospect of handsome reward.
De Thierry said: "The stock market is driven by the greed element, and ultimately people are going to forget about Bre-X."
